questions.prompt: Why did Joseph's brothers resent him so deeply?
choices: Their father loved him best and gave him a special tunic
He had taken over their father's flocks
He refused to work alongside them
He had married outside the family
questions.correctAnswer: Their father loved him best and gave him a special tunic
questions.explanation: Jacob's favoritism toward Joseph -- marked out by a special tunic -- is what curdles into his brothers' hatred. The family's own wound is what sets the rest of the story moving.
questions.hint: Their father made no secret of his favorite.

citations.quote: Israel loved Joseph best of all his sons, for he was the child of his old age, and he had made him a long ornamented tunic. When his brothers saw that their father loved him best of all his sons, they hated him so much that they would not even greet him.

questions.prompt: True or False: Joseph's brothers sold him into slavery rather than killing him outright.
questions.explanation: True. They agree to sell him to traders bound for Egypt instead of leaving him for dead -- a decision that, without anyone intending it, becomes the very road that later saves the family.
questions.hint: A trading caravan happened to be passing by.

citations.quote: They sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver, and they took him to Egypt.

questions.prompt: Joseph's brothers sold him to traders for twenty pieces of ____.
questions.explanation: A brother sold for silver by his own kin. Readers who already know the Gospels cannot help but hear an echo here, even though the Old Testament text stands complete on its own terms.
questions.hint: The same precious metal later paid to Judas.

citations.quote: They sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver, and they took him to Egypt.

questions.prompt: In Potiphar's house, what does Genesis say was the reason for Joseph's success?
choices: The Lord was with him
He had brought wealth with him from home
Potiphar owed his father a debt
He had won Pharaoh's favor beforehand
questions.explanation: Sold into a foreign house with nothing of his own, Joseph still prospers -- and the text is careful to say why: not his own cleverness alone, but that the Lord was with him.
questions.hint: The text names who was responsible, not just what Joseph did.

citations.quote: The LORD was with Joseph, and he prospered, and he lived in the house of his Egyptian master.

questions.prompt: True or False: Joseph is thrown into prison in Egypt because of a false accusation.
questions.explanation: True. Potiphar's wife accuses him falsely after he refuses her, and he is imprisoned for a wrong he did not commit -- innocent suffering, again, inside a story that keeps returning to that shape.
questions.hint: He is punished for something he refused to do, not something he did.

citations.quote: Joseph's master had him taken and put in the jail where the king's prisoners were confined.

questions.prompt: Match each stage of Joseph's descent to what happens there.

pairs.right: Loved above his brothers, given a special tunic
Sold by his own brothers for silver

questions.explanation: Each stage takes Joseph lower than the one before. The story will not turn upward again until the next level -- Egypt's whole future turns out to depend on the very man it had buried in a cell.
questions.hint: Each stage is a further fall from where he started.

citations.quote: They sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver, and they took him to Egypt.
Joseph's master had him taken and put in the jail where the king's prisoners were confined.

questions.prompt: What did Joseph's brothers do with his special tunic after selling him?
choices: Dipped it in goat's blood and brought it to their father
Burned it so no evidence would remain
Sold it along with Joseph himself
Buried it at the site of the pit
questions.correctAnswer: Dipped it in goat's blood and brought it to their father
questions.explanation: They let Jacob believe his favorite son was torn apart by a wild animal. The lie costs Jacob years of grief, and it is not undone until Joseph reveals himself many chapters later.
questions.hint: They needed their father to believe an animal was responsible.

citations.quote: Then they took Joseph's tunic, slaughtered a goat, and dipped the tunic in the blood. They had the ornamented tunic taken to their father

questions.prompt: True or False: Genesis says Joseph's brothers originally planned to kill him before one of them intervened.
questions.explanation: True. Reuben, the eldest, persuades the others to throw Joseph into a pit rather than kill him outright, intending secretly to rescue him later -- a plan that is overtaken when the others sell Joseph before Reuben returns.
questions.hint: One brother tried to save him, but was too slow.

citations.quote: When Reuben heard this, he tried to save him from their hands... Instead of taking his life... let him be thrown into that cistern here in the wilderness

questions.prompt: Genesis explains Joseph's success in Potiphar's house simply: 'The ____ was with Joseph, and he prospered.'
questions.explanation: The explanation the text gives is not Joseph's talent but God's presence with him, even in a foreign house, even as a slave with no standing of his own.
questions.hint: The text names who, not what.

citations.quote: The LORD was with Joseph, and he prospered, and he lived in the house of his Egyptian master.

questions.prompt: What theme connects Joseph's time in Potiphar's house and his time in prison?
choices: God's presence with him even in unjust suffering
His growing wealth and personal comfort
His brothers' continued involvement in his life
His plans to escape and return home
questions.correctAnswer: God's presence with him even in unjust suffering
questions.explanation: In both places Joseph is stripped of standing through no fault of his own, and in both places the text insists God has not left him. That insistence is what the rest of the story will vindicate.
questions.hint: In both places Joseph suffers a wrong he did not deserve.

citations.quote: The LORD was with Joseph, and he prospered, and he lived in the house of his Egyptian master.
Joseph's master had him taken and put in the jail where the king's prisoners were confined.

questions.prompt: How does Joseph come to Pharaoh's attention after years in prison?
choices: He interprets Pharaoh's troubling dreams
He petitions Pharaoh directly for release
His brothers arrive and vouch for him
Potiphar finally admits the accusation was false
questions.explanation: The same gift that first drew his brothers' resentment -- reading dreams -- is what finally lifts him out of prison. Nothing about Joseph has changed; only who is paying attention has.
questions.hint: The same gift that caused trouble with his brothers now serves him.

citations.quote: Pharaoh said to Joseph, 'I have had a dream, but no one can interpret it...' Joseph answered Pharaoh: 'It is not I, but God who will give Pharaoh a favorable answer.'

questions.prompt: True or False: When asked to interpret Pharaoh's dream, Joseph credits himself with the ability rather than God.
questions.explanation: False. Joseph is explicit: 'It is not I, but God who will give Pharaoh a favorable answer.' He refuses to take personal credit even at the moment his fortune is about to change entirely.
questions.hint: His actual answer names someone other than himself.

citations.quote: Pharaoh said to Joseph, 'I have had a dream, but no one can interpret it...' Joseph answered Pharaoh: 'It is not I, but God who will give Pharaoh a favorable answer.'

questions.prompt: Joseph tells Pharaoh: 'It is not I, but ____ who will give Pharaoh a favorable answer.'
questions.explanation: Even standing before the most powerful man in Egypt, Joseph redirects the credit. The pattern set at Potiphar's house -- 'the LORD was with Joseph' -- holds all the way to Pharaoh's throne.
questions.hint: He names who is really responsible for the answer.

citations.quote: Pharaoh said to Joseph, 'I have had a dream, but no one can interpret it...' Joseph answered Pharaoh: 'It is not I, but God who will give Pharaoh a favorable answer.'

questions.prompt: What position does Pharaoh give Joseph after his interpretation proves right?
choices: Second in command over all of Egypt
Governor of a single province
Chief steward of the royal household only
Commander of Pharaoh's army
questions.correctAnswer: Second in command over all of Egypt
questions.explanation: A man who was a slave and a prisoner within the same chapter is now set over the whole land, answerable to no one but Pharaoh himself. The reversal is total.
questions.hint: Pharaoh places him just below himself in authority.

citations.quote: You shall be over my house, and all my people shall dispose themselves as you command; only in respect to the throne will I outrank you. See, I have placed you in authority over all the land of Egypt.

questions.prompt: True or False: Joseph's rise to power in Egypt happens so that grain can be stored ahead of a coming famine.
questions.explanation: True. His interpretation of Pharaoh's dream warns of seven years of famine after seven years of plenty, and his administration is what saves Egypt -- and, eventually, his own family -- from starvation.
questions.hint: Pharaoh's dream itself was a warning about food.

citations.quote: You shall be over my house, and all my people shall dispose themselves as you command; only in respect to the throne will I outrank you. See, I have placed you in authority over all the land of Egypt.

questions.prompt: Match each stage of Joseph's rise to what enables it.

pairs.right: Given entirely to God, not himself
Prepares Egypt for the famine ahead

questions.explanation: The same gift that made his brothers resent him now saves a nation. Nothing in Joseph has changed since the pit -- only the use his gift has finally been put to.
questions.hint: Each item on the left leads directly to the one beside it.

citations.quote: Pharaoh said to Joseph, 'I have had a dream, but no one can interpret it...' Joseph answered Pharaoh: 'It is not I, but God who will give Pharaoh a favorable answer.'

You shall be over my house, and all my people shall dispose themselves as you command; only in respect to the throne will I outrank you. See, I have placed you in authority over all the land of Egypt.

questions.prompt: How old was Joseph, according to Genesis, when he entered Pharaoh's service?
choices: Thirty
Seventeen
Forty
Twenty-five
questions.explanation: He was seventeen when his brothers sold him. More than a decade of slavery and imprisonment passes before Pharaoh ever hears of him -- the reversal did not come quickly.
questions.hint: More than a decade has passed since he was sold at seventeen.

citations.quote: Joseph was thirty years old when he entered the service of Pharaoh, king of Egypt.

questions.prompt: True or False: More than a decade passed between Joseph being sold into slavery and his rise to power in Egypt.
questions.explanation: True. Sold at seventeen, elevated at thirty -- thirteen years pass in slavery and prison before the reversal comes. The story does not rush past Joseph's long wait.
questions.hint: Compare the two ages Genesis gives for him.

citations.quote: Joseph was thirty years old when he entered the service of Pharaoh, king of Egypt.

questions.prompt: Pharaoh tells Joseph: 'Only in respect to the ____ will I outrank you.'
questions.explanation: Pharaoh sets Joseph over everything except the throne itself. It is as near to total authority as Egypt can grant to anyone who is not Pharaoh.
questions.hint: The one thing Pharaoh does not hand over.

citations.quote: You shall be over my house, and all my people shall dispose themselves as you command; only in respect to the throne will I outrank you. See, I have placed you in authority over all the land of Egypt.

questions.prompt: What does Joseph's long wait between the pit and the palace suggest about how the promise to Abraham unfolds?
choices: God's plan can move through long delay and real suffering
God's plan always moves quickly once begun
Suffering is a sign that a person has been abandoned
The promise to Abraham had nothing to do with Joseph
questions.correctAnswer: God's plan can move through long delay and real suffering
questions.explanation: Thirteen years is a long time to wait in a foreign prison. The pattern set with Abraham -- promises kept across long stretches of ordinary, unremarkable time -- holds true again here.
questions.hint: Consider how long Joseph waited, and what the wait cost him.

citations.quote: Joseph was thirty years old when he entered the service of Pharaoh, king of Egypt.
The patriarchs, prophets and certain other Old Testament figures have been and always will be honored as saints in all the Church's liturgical traditions.

questions.prompt: Why do Joseph's brothers travel to Egypt years later, not recognizing him?
choices: Famine has struck Canaan and Egypt has grain
They are searching for Joseph himself
Jacob has sent them to make peace with Egypt
They are fleeing an enemy army
questions.correctAnswer: Famine has struck Canaan and Egypt has grain
questions.explanation: The very famine Joseph's administration prepared for is what drives his own family, unknowing, into his presence. What began as betrayal is quietly becoming the means of their survival.
questions.hint: What did Joseph spend seven years storing up?

citations.quote: When Jacob learned that grain rations were available in Egypt, he said to his sons... Ten of Joseph's brothers, then, went down to procure grain rations in Egypt.

questions.prompt: True or False: When Joseph finally reveals himself to his brothers, he tells them not to be distressed, because God sent him ahead to preserve life.
questions.explanation: True. Joseph reframes the whole story without denying what his brothers actually did -- he names God's purpose working through their betrayal, not in place of it.
questions.hint: He reinterprets what happened rather than pretending it didn't.

citations.quote: But now do not be distressed, and do not be angry with yourselves for having sold me here. It was really for the sake of saving lives that God sent me here ahead of you.

questions.prompt: At the end of Genesis, Joseph tells his brothers: 'You meant evil against me, but God meant it for ____.'
questions.explanation: This single sentence is the key to the whole Joseph cycle, and it is the shape the Church will later see filled out completely at the cross: real evil, freely done, that God does not merely permit but turns to save many lives.
questions.hint: The word names the opposite of what his brothers intended.

citations.quote: Even though you meant harm to me, God meant it for good, to achieve his present end, the survival of many people.

questions.prompt: According to Genesis 50:20, what did God's turning of evil into good actually achieve?
choices: The survival of many people
The punishment of Joseph's brothers
The restoration of Joseph's original tunic
The immediate return of the family to Canaan
questions.explanation: Joseph's suffering is not undone by this sentence -- it is given a purpose beyond what anyone intended when they threw him into the pit: the saving of many lives, his own family's among them.
questions.hint: The purpose named is about people staying alive.

citations.quote: Even though you meant harm to me, God meant it for good, to achieve his present end, the survival of many people.

questions.prompt: True or False: Because of Joseph, Jacob and his entire family come to live in Egypt.
questions.explanation: True. The famine and Joseph's position bring the whole family down into Egypt, where they settle and grow -- setting the stage for the very different situation the next level of this topic will open with.
questions.hint: Think about where the family ends up living by the end of Genesis.

citations.quote: But now do not be distressed, and do not be angry with yourselves for having sold me here. It was really for the sake of saving lives that God sent me here ahead of you.

questions.prompt: Match each moment of the reunion to what it accomplishes.

pairs.right: Brings the brothers to Egypt for grain
Names God's purpose in their betrayal
Sets up the situation the next level opens with

questions.explanation: Every earlier low point in Joseph's story is answered here: the pit, the false accusation, the years in prison. None of it is denied -- all of it is given a purpose larger than what anyone intended.
questions.hint: Read left to right as consequence, not coincidence.

citations.quote: But now do not be distressed, and do not be angry with yourselves for having sold me here. It was really for the sake of saving lives that God sent me here ahead of you.
Even though you meant harm to me, God meant it for good, to achieve his present end, the survival of many people.

questions.prompt: What makes Joseph's response to his brothers different from simple forgiveness alone?
choices: He names a divine purpose at work in what they did
He refuses to speak to them at all
He demands they repay what they took from him
He denies that anything wrong happened
questions.correctAnswer: He names a divine purpose at work in what they did
questions.explanation: Joseph does not simply say 'I forgive you' and leave it there. He reinterprets the entire event theologically -- real wrong, freely chosen, and God's purpose accomplished through it rather than around it.
questions.hint: He does more than say the wrong is behind them.

citations.quote: Even though you meant harm to me, God meant it for good, to achieve his present end, the survival of many people.

questions.prompt: True or False: Genesis 50:20 is often read by the Church as an early pattern for how God works through the Cross.
questions.explanation: True. A real evil, freely done by real people, that God does not merely tolerate but works through to save many -- that is exactly the shape the Church sees completed at Calvary.
questions.hint: Think about what else in Scripture involves real evil turned to the saving of many.

citations.quote: Even though you meant harm to me, God meant it for good, to achieve his present end, the survival of many people.

The Church... has illuminated the unity of the divine plan in the two Testaments through typology, which discerns in God's works of the Old Covenant prefigurations of what he accomplished in the fullness of time in the person of his incarnate Son.

questions.prompt: Joseph tells his brothers it was for the sake of ____ lives that God sent him ahead of them.
questions.explanation: The purpose Joseph names is rescue, not revenge. It is the same purpose the whole Old Testament has been building toward since the first promise in the garden.
questions.hint: The purpose is about keeping people alive.

citations.quote: But now do not be distressed, and do not be angry with yourselves for having sold me here. It was really for the sake of saving lives that God sent me here ahead of you.

questions.prompt: Looking back over Joseph's whole story, what does it demonstrate about how the promise to Abraham keeps moving forward?
choices: Through ordinary human choices, even cruel ones, that God does not override but works through
Only through direct miracles that bypass human freedom entirely
Only through kings and prophets, never through family conflict
It stalls completely until Moses is born
questions.correctAnswer: Through ordinary human choices, even cruel ones, that God does not override but works through
questions.explanation: Nobody in this story does anything supernatural. Jealous brothers, a slave trade, a false accusation, a forgotten prisoner -- ordinary cruelty and ordinary mercy, and the promise to Abraham moves forward through all of it.
questions.hint: Notice how few miracles actually happen in this whole story.

citations.quote: Even though you meant harm to me, God meant it for good, to achieve his present end, the survival of many people.
